title: "Core panel models"
---

::: {.callout-note}
**Placeholder.** This chapter is planned, not written. Tracked in the node
checklist in [the preface](../../index.qmd).
:::

This chapter steps back from dependence, spatial or cross-sectional, and asks
the questions a panel raises on its own: can the units be pooled into one
regression, do fixed or random effects fit better, and are the standard
errors trustworthy. Chapters
[cross-sectional dependence](../02-cross-dependence/index.qmd),
[spatial dependence](../03-spatial/index.qmd) and
[time dependence](../04-time/index.qmd) already lean on fixed-effects
residuals before this chapter explains what fixed effects assume and when
random effects is the better choice; this chapter is where that gloss is
redeemed.

**Planned sections.** Numbers in brackets refer to
`.docs/panel-spat-PLAN.md`.

1. **Poolability.** Can one regression serve every unit, or does each need
   its own intercept and slopes? The classical Chow-type F test and Swamy's
   random-coefficients alternative (3.1).
2. **Slope homogeneity.** A modern alternative to poolability, the
   Pesaran–Yamagata Δ tests, built for the N large, T moderate case (3.2).
3. **Heteroskedasticity.** Testing for it, and why its presence routes
   spatial estimation toward IV and GMM instead of maximum likelihood (3.3).
4. **Effects tests.** Breusch–Pagan LM, Honda, and the conditional LM family
   decide whether fixed or random effects beat pooled OLS at all (4a.1).
5. **Fixed vs random effects.** The Hausman test and its robust variants,
   plus the two-way case and its five distinct hypotheses (4a.2).
6. **Robust standard errors.** Driscoll–Kraay, Beck–Katz, and clustered
   variants for the dependence a plain vcov misses (4a.4).
